  — *Why this level:* Defining what excellent API storytelling through code means and shaping external practice is Dreyfus's master band -- the discipline-setting level Docs for Developers' authors themselves work at. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Bhatti, Corleissen, Lambourne, Nunez & Waterhouse, Docs for Developers: An Engineer's Field Guide to Technical Writing (Apress, 2021).

### Product & Delivery (PD)

#### Value Delivery

<a id="pd-01"></a>
##### PD-01 — Work Breakdown & Incremental Delivery

*Type:* Behavioral — Slices work so value and learning arrive early.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Breaks own tasks into reviewable pieces with guidance.
  — *Why this level:* Breaking own tasks into reviewable pieces with guidance is the novice band -- slicing at the individual-task level, with someone else checking each slice. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Independently decomposes a feature into shippable slices.
  — *Why this level:* Independently decomposing a feature into shippable slices is the advanced-beginner band, applying the Agile Manifesto's preference for frequent delivery of working software to a known feature. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Beck et al., Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Plans complex multi-phase work (prototype-then-commit under uncertainty); sequences safely.
  — *Why this level:* Planning complex multi-phase work under uncertainty and sequencing it safely is the competent band and is what Patton's story mapping is built to do -- hold the whole story while choosing a safe walking skeleton to build first. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Patton, User Story Mapping: Discover the Whole Story, Build the Right Product (O'Reilly, 2014).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Expert at structuring large initiatives to de-risk early; anticipates bottlenecks.
  — *Why this level:* Structuring large initiatives to de-risk early and anticipating bottlenecks moves from slicing a feature to designing a release strategy -- the kind of decoupled, staged rollout feature toggles are built to support and continuous delivery pipelines make safe. *Sources:* Hodgson, Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags) (martinfowler.com, 2017); Humble & Farley, Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build Test and Deployment Automation (Addison-Wesley, 2010).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Shapes how the org plans and sequences major change.
  — *Why this level:* Shaping how the org plans and sequences major change is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- setting delivery approach across programs, not one initiative. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines the company-wide approach to delivering value incrementally.
  — *Why this level:* Defining the company-wide approach to delivering value incrementally is Dreyfus's master band; Patton's story-mapping technique itself became this kind of company-wide default after his book. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Patton, User Story Mapping: Discover the Whole Story, Build the Right Product (O'Reilly, 2014).

<a id="pd-02"></a>
##### PD-02 — Prioritization & Economic Thinking

*Type:* Behavioral — Weighs cost, value, risk and timing.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Works highest-priority-first when told the priorities.
  — *Why this level:* Working highest-priority-first when told the priorities is the novice band -- executing someone else's ranking, not producing one. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Makes sound priority calls within scope; time-boxes uncertain work.
  — *Why this level:* Making sound priority calls within scope and time-boxing uncertain work is the advanced-beginner band, applying basic cost/value trade-offs inside a bounded area. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Boehm, Software Engineering Economics (Prentice-Hall, 1981).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Balances cost/value/risk across a domain; resists hype; decisions hold up over months.
  — *Why this level:* Balancing cost/value/risk across a domain so decisions hold up over months is the competent band and is what Reinertsen's cost-of-delay economics is built to make explicit -- quantifying trade-offs instead of arguing them by instinct. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development (Celeritas, 2009).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Expert at portfolio-level trade-offs; surfaces hidden assumptions; trusted tiebreaker.
  — *Why this level:* Expert-level portfolio trade-offs and surfacing hidden assumptions is Reinertsen's queueing-and-batch-size economics applied across a portfolio, not one project -- the point at which prioritization requires modeling flow, not just ranking a backlog. *Sources:* Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development (Celeritas, 2009).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets decision frameworks for the org.
  — *Why this level:* Setting decision frameworks for the org is SFIA9's strategic-influence band combined with Boehm's software-economics case for codifying how an organization values trade-offs, not just making one. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Boehm, Software Engineering Economics (Prentice-Hall, 1981).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Influences company strategic direction through judgment.
  — *Why this level:* Influencing company strategic direction through judgment is Dreyfus's master band -- prioritization reasoning that shapes strategy itself, the level Reinertsen argues most organizations never reach. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development (Celeritas, 2009).

<a id="pd-03"></a>
##### PD-03 — Dealing with Ambiguity

*Type:* Behavioral — Makes progress when the problem is unclear.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Asks good questions to turn a vague task into a clear one.
  — *Why this level:* Asking good questions to turn a vague task into a clear one is the novice band -- the Cynefin move of first recognizing you're not in the simple domain, then asking for help mapping it. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review 85(11), 68-76 (2007).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Independently turns a vague request into a workable plan.
  — *Why this level:* Independently turning a vague request into a workable plan is the advanced-beginner band, self-sufficient in Cynefin's complicated domain -- knowable with analysis -- but not yet the complex domain. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review 85(11), 68-76 (2007).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Thrives in ambiguity; frames the problem for others; chooses an approach and commits.
  — *Why this level:* Thriving in ambiguity, framing the problem for others, and committing to an approach is the competent band and is exactly Cynefin's complex-domain leadership move -- probe-sense-respond because cause and effect are only clear in hindsight. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review 85(11), 68-76 (2007).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Creates clarity for multiple teams out of open-ended situations.
  — *Why this level:* Creating clarity for multiple teams out of open-ended situations extends Cynefin's complex-domain framing across several teams' worth of ambiguity at once, not just one's own. *Sources:* Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review 85(11), 68-76 (2007).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Defines direction where none exists at org scale.
  — *Why this level:* Defining direction where none exists at org scale is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- the leader Snowden and Boone describe operating routinely in the chaotic domain and acting first to establish order. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review 85(11), 68-76 (2007).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Comfortable with the highest-uncertainty company bets.
  — *Why this level:* Comfortable with the highest-uncertainty company bets is Dreyfus's master band -- sustained operation in Cynefin's chaotic quadrant where no framework yet applies. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review 85(11), 68-76 (2007).

#### Execution

<a id="pd-04"></a>
##### PD-04 — Estimation & Planning

*Type:* Behavioral — Forecasts and plans work credibly.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Learns to estimate; surfaces blockers; plans own tasks with guidance.
  — *Why this level:* Learning to estimate, surfacing blockers, and planning own tasks with guidance is the novice band -- following an estimation technique under someone else's check. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning (Prentice Hall, 2005).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Estimates scoped work realistically; plans own 1-3 week projects.
  — *Why this level:* Estimating scoped work realistically and planning own 1-3 week projects is the advanced-beginner band, applying Cohn's relative-sizing and velocity techniques independently within a known scope. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning (Prentice Hall, 2005).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Plans quarter-scale, multi-workstream efforts including dependencies.
  — *Why this level:* Planning quarter-scale, multi-workstream efforts including dependencies is the competent band and requires Cohn's release-planning layer, not just iteration planning -- sequencing across workstreams with dependencies. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cohn, Agile Estimating and Planning (Prentice Hall, 2005).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Expert at planning large programs; anticipates risk early.
  — *Why this level:* Expert-level planning of large programs that anticipates risk early is what PMBOK's performance domains formalize for program-scale planning -- planning where the work itself spans multiple teams' plans. *Sources:* Project Management Institute, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), 7th ed. (PMI, 2021).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Plans org-level programs across quarters/years.
  — *Why this level:* Planning org-level programs across quarters and years is SFIA9's strategic-influence band paired with PMBOK's standard for value-delivery planning at portfolio scale. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Project Management Institute, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), 7th ed. (PMI, 2021).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Shapes how the company plans major technical change.
  — *Why this level:* Shaping how the company plans major technical change is Dreyfus's master band -- setting the planning method itself, the level a body of knowledge like PMBOK codifies from industry practice. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Project Management Institute, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), 7th ed. (PMI, 2021).

<a id="pd-05"></a>
##### PD-05 — Ownership & Delivery Accountability

*Type:* Behavioral — Makes and keeps credible commitments.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Takes ownership of assigned tasks; honest about progress and blockers.
  — *Why this level:* Taking ownership of assigned tasks and being honest about progress and blockers is the novice band -- ownership scoped to one's own work, with visible reporting. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Owns components end-to-end; delivers committed work reliably.
  — *Why this level:* Owning components end-to-end and delivering committed work reliably is the advanced-beginner band, applying Willink & Babin's baseline of taking ownership of outcomes rather than excuses to a bounded component. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Willink & Babin, Extreme Ownership: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win (St. Martin's Press, 2015).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Owns a domain; lands multi-week efforts without surprises; pushes back on unrealistic scope with reasons.
  — *Why this level:* Owning a domain, landing multi-week efforts without surprises, and pushing back on unrealistic scope with reasons is the competent band -- Willink & Babin's ownership principle extended to a whole delivery domain, not a single task. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Willink & Babin, Extreme Ownership: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win (St. Martin's Press, 2015).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Owns cross-team initiatives; unblocks teams; kills failing approaches early.
  — *Why this level:* Owning cross-team initiatives, unblocking teams, and killing failing approaches early is ownership extended across teams the way Willink & Babin describe commanders owning outcomes beyond their own unit, and matches what DORA's research finds distinguishes high-performing delivery organizations. *Sources:* Willink & Babin, Extreme Ownership: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win (St. Martin's Press, 2015); DORA (Google Cloud), Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Owns an org-level portfolio of bets; sets direction others follow.
  — *Why this level:* Owning an org-level portfolio of bets and setting direction others follow is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- accountability at the scale of a portfolio, not a program. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** The go-to when something company-critical must land.
  — *Why this level:* Being the go-to when something company-critical must land is Dreyfus's master band -- the level of trust Willink & Babin describe reserved for leaders proven under the highest stakes. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Willink & Babin, Extreme Ownership: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win (St. Martin's Press, 2015).

<a id="pd-06"></a>
##### PD-06 — Product Thinking

*Type:* Behavioral — Connects technical work to user and business value.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Understands the capability they're building and who uses it.
  — *Why this level:* Understanding the capability they're building and who uses it is the novice band -- user awareness without yet making product decisions. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Frames own work in user/business outcomes, not just tasks.
  — *Why this level:* Framing own work in user/business outcomes, not just tasks, is the advanced-beginner band -- Cagan's baseline expectation that engineers understand the outcome their work serves, without yet owning discovery. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cagan, INSPIRED: How to Create Tech Products Customers Love, 2nd Edition (Wiley, 2018).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Treats their area as a product; uses metrics to decide what to build for a domain.
  — *Why this level:* Treating their area as a product and using metrics to decide what to build for a domain is the competent band and is Torres's continuous-discovery habit of weekly customer contact driving build decisions -- not a one-time discovery phase. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Torres, Continuous Discovery Habits: Discover Products that Create Customer Value and Business Value (Product Talk LLC, 2021).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Expert at aligning technical bets with product strategy across teams.
  — *Why this level:* Expert alignment of technical bets with product strategy across teams is Cagan's account of product leaders who connect strategy to multiple teams' roadmaps, beyond running one team's discovery. *Sources:* Cagan, INSPIRED: How to Create Tech Products Customers Love, 2nd Edition (Wiley, 2018).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets product direction for an org's technical surface.
  — *Why this level:* Setting product direction for an org's technical surface is SFIA9's strategic-influence band combined with Perri's case for product strategy that ties vision to economic outcomes org-wide. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Perri, Escaping the Build Trap: How Effective Product Management Creates Real Value (O'Reilly, 2018).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Shapes how the company creates value through technical products.
  — *Why this level:* Shaping how the company creates value through technical products is Dreyfus's master band -- escaping the build trap at company scale, the transformation Perri's book is written to drive. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Perri, Escaping the Build Trap: How Effective Product Management Creates Real Value (O'Reilly, 2018).

<a id="pd-07"></a>
##### PD-07 — Strategic & Commercial Awareness

*Type:* Behavioral — Frames technical decisions in economic and business terms — cost, revenue risk, cost of delay, unit economics — and answers for whether the work actually moved its business outcome.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** States what business outcome their current task serves — and asks when they can't — treating infrastructure and license costs as real money.
  — *Why this level:* Stating what business outcome their current task serves, and treating infrastructure/license costs as real money, is the novice band -- cost-awareness at the level FinOps calls informing: seeing the numbers, not yet acting on them. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Checks whether shipped work actually moved its metric and says so plainly when it didn't; weighs cost and maintenance burden in the technical choices they own.
  — *Why this level:* Checking whether shipped work actually moved its metric and weighing cost/maintenance burden in owned technical choices is the advanced-beginner band -- FinOps's optimizing phase applied to work one owns directly. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Frames a domain's technical decisions in business terms — cost of delay, revenue risk, support load — pushes back on work with weak business rationale, and redirects effort when the numbers say the plan is wrong.
  — *Why this level:* Framing a domain's technical decisions in cost-of-delay and revenue-risk terms, and redirecting effort when the numbers say the plan is wrong, is the competent band and is Reinertsen's economic-framework case for making cost of delay the single unit of measure for technical trade-offs. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development (Celeritas, 2009).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Builds the business case for the cross-team technical investments with the largest return and is trusted by leadership to have done the math.
  — *Why this level:* Building the business case for cross-team technical investments with the largest return is Boehm's software-economics tradition of quantifying engineering investment in business terms applied at cross-team scale. *Sources:* Boehm, Software Engineering Economics (Prentice-Hall, 1981).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Aligns an organization's technical strategy with its economics — cost curves, velocity, risk — owning trade-offs measured in staff-years and reporting them in the business's own terms.
  — *Why this level:* Aligning an org's technical strategy with its economics -- cost curves, velocity, risk -- is SFIA9's strategic-influence band paired with FinOps's operate-at-scale maturity, where cost accountability is owned organization-wide. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); FinOps Foundation, FinOps Framework (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Advises company leadership on where technology changes the business model and is accountable for company-level technology bets paying off.
  — *Why this level:* Advising company leadership on where technology changes the business model is Dreyfus's master band -- the level Perri argues separates feature factories from companies where product/technology strategy IS business strategy. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Perri, Escaping the Build Trap: How Effective Product Management Creates Real Value (O'Reilly, 2018).

### Communication & Collaboration (CC)

#### Communication

<a id="cc-01"></a>
##### CC-01 — Written & Verbal Communication

*Type:* Behavioral — Conveys ideas clearly to the right audience.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Communicates status clearly; documentation is accurate.
  — *Why this level:* Communicating status clearly with accurate documentation is the novice band -- Zinsser's baseline clarity discipline: say what happened, plainly. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Zinsser, On Writing Well: The Classic Guide to Writing Nonfiction, 30th Anniversary Edition (Harper Perennial, 2006).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Writes clear design notes, runbooks and PRs; explains trade-offs without overselling.
  — *Why this level:* Writing clear design notes, runbooks and PRs, and explaining trade-offs without overselling, is the advanced-beginner band -- Zinsser's 'clutter is the disease' discipline applied to routine technical writing. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Zinsser, On Writing Well: The Classic Guide to Writing Nonfiction, 30th Anniversary Edition (Harper Perennial, 2006).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Writes design docs that drive decisions; translates technical risk for non-technical stakeholders.
  — *Why this level:* Writing design docs that drive decisions and translating technical risk for non-technical stakeholders is the competent band and requires Minto's answer-first, pyramid-structured argument -- leading with the conclusion a decision-maker needs. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking, and Problem Solving (Minto International, 1996).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Expert at making complex capability/risk legible to executives without dumbing it down; RFCs align orgs.
  — *Why this level:* Making complex capability/risk legible to executives without dumbing it down, and having RFCs align orgs, is Minto's pyramid principle applied at the scale of documents that must persuade rooms full of stakeholders at once. *Sources:* Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking, and Problem Solving (Minto International, 1996).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Strategy memos leadership acts on; org-wide and external reach.
  — *Why this level:* Strategy memos leadership acts on, with org-wide and external reach, is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- writing that changes org direction, not just informs it. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** A clarifying voice at company scale; externally recognized.
  — *Why this level:* Being a clarifying voice at company scale, externally recognized, is Dreyfus's master band -- the level Zinsser's decades of teaching writers aimed to reach: clarity that carries beyond one's own organization. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Zinsser, On Writing Well: The Classic Guide to Writing Nonfiction, 30th Anniversary Edition (Harper Perennial, 2006).

<a id="cc-02"></a>
##### CC-02 — Knowledge Sharing & Documentation

*Type:* Behavioral — Spreads understanding so others move faster.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Shares what they learn; keeps their docs accurate.
  — *Why this level:* Sharing what they learn and keeping their docs accurate is the novice band -- Stepper's first Working Out Loud habit of simply making one's work visible. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Stepper, Working Out Loud: For a Better Career and Life (Ikigai Press, 2015).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Documents their area well; proactively shares techniques with the team.
  — *Why this level:* Documenting their area well and proactively sharing techniques with the team is the advanced-beginner band -- Stepper's narrating-work practice extended into a habit, not a one-off post. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Stepper, Working Out Loud: For a Better Career and Life (Ikigai Press, 2015).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Creates documentation and forums that raise a whole domain's understanding.
  — *Why this level:* Creating documentation and forums that raise a whole domain's understanding is the competent band -- Stepper's relationship-building through visible work scaled to a domain of people, not just individual narration. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Stepper, Working Out Loud: For a Better Career and Life (Ikigai Press, 2015).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Builds knowledge-sharing systems adopted across teams.
  — *Why this level:* Building knowledge-sharing systems adopted across teams moves from personal practice to institutional infrastructure -- the kind of documented, org-wide practice published career ladders like GitLab's expect at senior engineering levels. *Sources:* GitLab Handbook, Engineering Management Job Framework (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Defines how the org captures and spreads knowledge.
  — *Why this level:* Defining how the org captures and spreads knowledge is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- designing the knowledge system, not populating it. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Shapes industry-facing knowledge practice.
  — *Why this level:* Shaping industry-facing knowledge practice is Dreyfus's master band -- the level at which a practice like Working Out Loud becomes an externally adopted movement rather than one person's habit. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Stepper, Working Out Loud: For a Better Career and Life (Ikigai Press, 2015).

#### Collaboration

<a id="cc-03"></a>
##### CC-03 — Teamwork & Partnership

*Type:* Behavioral — Works productively with others toward shared goals.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Responsive to feedback; pairs willingly; asks for help appropriately.
  — *Why this level:* Being responsive to feedback, pairing willingly, and asking for help appropriately is the novice band -- the trust-building forming stage of Tuckman's model, taken individually. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Tuckman, Developmental Sequence in Small Groups, Psychological Bulletin 63(6), 384-399 (1965).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Collaborates smoothly with adjacent functions; handles disagreement constructively.
  — *Why this level:* Collaborating smoothly with adjacent functions and handling disagreement constructively is the advanced-beginner band -- navigating Tuckman's storming stage without derailing the team. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Tuckman, Developmental Sequence in Small Groups, Psychological Bulletin 63(6), 384-399 (1965).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Builds strong cross-team relationships; resolves friction directly.
  — *Why this level:* Building strong cross-team relationships and resolving friction directly is the competent band and is Lencioni's trust-and-conflict foundation applied across team boundaries -- the first two dysfunctions actively countered, not just avoided. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team: A Leadership Fable (Jossey-Bass, 2002).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Expert at aligning teams with competing priorities; mediates disputes between senior people.
  — *Why this level:* Aligning teams with competing priorities and mediating disputes between senior people is Lencioni's dysfunction model applied where accountability and results are contested between teams, not individuals -- resolving the harder, structural dysfunctions. *Sources:* Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team: A Leadership Fable (Jossey-Bass, 2002).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Creates the forums and processes through which collaboration happens.
  — *Why this level:* Creating the forums and processes through which collaboration happens is SFIA9's strategic-influence band combined with Team Topologies' case for deliberately designing team interaction modes rather than letting them emerge. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Skelton & Pais, Team Topologies (IT Revolution, 2019).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Builds coalitions at company scale and externally.
  — *Why this level:* Building coalitions at company scale and externally is Dreyfus's master band -- sustained, healthy team function beyond any one team, the outcome Lencioni's model is built to produce at scale. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Lencioni, The Five Dysfunctions of a Team: A Leadership Fable (Jossey-Bass, 2002).

<a id="cc-04"></a>
##### CC-04 — Feedback

*Type:* Behavioral — Gives and receives honest, useful feedback.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Accepts feedback non-defensively; acts on it.
  — *Why this level:* Accepting feedback non-defensively and acting on it is the novice band -- the receiving-feedback skill Stone & Heen treat as foundational and non-trivial, not something people arrive already good at. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Stone & Heen, Thanks for the Feedback: The Science and Art of Receiving Feedback Well (Viking, 2014).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Gives timely, specific, kind feedback to peers.
  — *Why this level:* Giving timely, specific, kind feedback to peers is the advanced-beginner band -- Scott's 'care personally, challenge directly' quadrant applied to routine peer feedback. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Scott, Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity (St. Martin's Press, 2017).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Gives growth-oriented feedback that changes behavior; coaches through feedback.
  — *Why this level:* Giving growth-oriented feedback that changes behavior, coaching through feedback, is the competent band and is Radical Candor's harder discipline -- challenging directly enough that behavior actually changes, not just noting the issue. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Scott, Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity (St. Martin's Press, 2017).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Builds feedback norms that raise the bar across teams.
  — *Why this level:* Building feedback norms that raise the bar across teams is Radical Candor applied as an instituted team practice rather than one person's individual habit -- norms others are held to. *Sources:* Scott, Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity (St. Martin's Press, 2017).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the org's culture of candor and growth.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the org's culture of candor and growth is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- Scott's own argument that radical candor has to be modeled and built into culture from leadership down, not left to individual managers. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Scott, Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity (St. Martin's Press, 2017).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Models and defines feedback culture company-wide.
  — *Why this level:* Modeling and defining feedback culture company-wide is Dreyfus's master band -- the level at which a leader's feedback practice becomes the company's, the aim Scott's book sets for its readers. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Scott, Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity (St. Martin's Press, 2017).

<a id="cc-05"></a>
##### CC-05 — Handling Disagreement

*Type:* Behavioral — Navigates conflict toward good decisions.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Voices disagreement respectfully; disagrees-and-commits.
  — *Why this level:* Voicing disagreement respectfully and disagreeing-and-committing is the novice band -- Fisher & Ury's baseline of separating people from the problem, practiced individually. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Fisher & Ury, Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In (Penguin, 1981).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Works through disagreement to a decision without damaging relationships.
  — *Why this level:* Working through disagreement to a decision without damaging relationships is the advanced-beginner band -- applying principled-negotiation moves to reach a decision, not just state a position. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Fisher & Ury, Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In (Penguin, 1981).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Mediates technical disputes in their domain; finds the path that holds up.
  — *Why this level:* Mediating technical disputes in their domain and finding the path that holds up is the competent band and is what Crucial Conversations calls stepping into dialogue when stakes, opinions, and emotions are all high -- mediating, not just negotiating one's own position. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler, Crucial Conversations: Tools for Talking When Stakes Are High, 2nd Edition (McGraw-Hill, 2011).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Resolves high-stakes disagreements between senior stakeholders across orgs.
  — *Why this level:* Resolving high-stakes disagreements between senior stakeholders across orgs is Crucial Conversations' toolkit applied where the stakes and organizational distance are both highest. *Sources:* Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler, Crucial Conversations: Tools for Talking When Stakes Are High, 2nd Edition (McGraw-Hill, 2011).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Designs the decision processes the org uses to resolve conflict.
  — *Why this level:* Designing the decision processes the org uses to resolve conflict is SFIA9's strategic-influence band -- building the structure for disagreement to resolve well, not resolving each instance personally. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Sets the company norm for principled disagreement.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the company norm for principled disagreement is Dreyfus's master band -- the level at which Fisher & Ury's 'insist on objective criteria' becomes how a whole company disagrees, not one negotiator's technique. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Fisher & Ury, Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In (Penguin, 1981).

#### Communication

<a id="cc-06"></a>
##### CC-06 — Executive Communication

*Type:* Behavioral — Communicates upward and to executive audiences — answer-first briefings, decision-ready framing, and composure under hostile questioning.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Prepares status updates for leadership with guidance; leads with the headline when coached to.
  — *Why this level:* Preparing status updates for leadership with guidance, leading with the headline when coached to, is the novice band -- following Minto's answer-first structure because someone reminds them to, not yet by habit. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking, and Problem Solving (Minto International, 1996).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Reports upward answer-first with a specific ask; escalates early with options attached, so no surprise reaches leadership from someone else.
  — *Why this level:* Reporting upward answer-first with a specific ask, escalating early with options attached, is the advanced-beginner band -- Minto's pyramid principle applied as a self-sufficient habit. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking, and Problem Solving (Minto International, 1996).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Briefs senior leaders under pressure — facts, impact, options, and a recommendation inside the first two minutes; one-pagers get forwarded unedited.
  — *Why this level:* Briefing senior leaders under pressure with facts, impact, options, and a recommendation inside two minutes is the competent band and is Grove's case for a manager's output being measured in the output of the organizations under their influence -- communication precise enough to drive that output without wasting a leader's attention. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Grove, High Output Management (Random House, 1983).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Builds and lands investment cases with executive audiences — pre-wired with skeptics, sized in business terms, honest about risk; coaches others for executive rooms and runs the operating reviews an organization communicates through.
  — *Why this level:* Building and landing investment cases with executive audiences, pre-wired with skeptics and sized in business terms, is Minto's pyramid principle deployed at the scale of a decision that must survive hostile scrutiny, plus coaching others to do the same. *Sources:* Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing, Thinking, and Problem Solving (Minto International, 1996).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Operates the executive room as a peer — advances positions, absorbs hostile questioning without defensiveness, and changes the room's decision more often than not.
  — *Why this level:* Operating the executive room as a peer, absorbing hostile questioning and changing the room's decision, is SFIA9's highest strategic-influence band combined with Grove's account of the high-leverage activities -- like decisions made in meetings among peers -- that define senior management work. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Grove, High Output Management (Random House, 1983).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Speaks for an organization's technical reality to boards, investors, and press; trusted with the messages that cannot be delegated, and organizational credibility survives the appearances.
  — *Why this level:* Speaking for an organization's technical reality to boards, investors, and press, with organizational credibility on the line, is Dreyfus's master band -- Grove's output-of-a-manager principle extended to speaking for the organization's credibility itself. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Grove, High Output Management (Random House, 1983).

### Leadership & Influence (LI)

#### Growing People

<a id="li-01"></a>
##### LI-01 — Mentorship & Coaching

*Type:* Behavioral — Grows other people's capability.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Receptive to mentoring; shares what they learn.
  — *Why this level:* Being receptive to mentoring and passing along what one learns is the receiving end of Kram's developmental-relationship functions before a person provides them to others; Dreyfus places this observation-and-uptake stance at the novice band, where the learner still needs the relationship supplied rather than initiating it. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kram, Mentoring at Work: Developmental Relationships in Organizational Life (Scott Foresman, 1985).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Helps onboard teammates; informally mentors juniors.
  — *Why this level:* Informally offering the psychosocial and career-support functions Kram documents -- without yet being asked to own someone's development -- is the advanced-beginner transition from receiving mentoring to giving it, in bounded, low-stakes situations like onboarding. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kram, Mentoring at Work: Developmental Relationships in Organizational Life (Scott Foresman, 1985).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Coaches engineers with growth-oriented feedback; measurably improves a team's skill.
  — *Why this level:* Deliberately using Kram's coaching and challenging functions to produce a measurable skill change is the competent band's autonomous, go-to coaching Dreyfus describes; SFIA's mid-band responsibility for developing team members' skills matches the same team-scoped ownership. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kram, Mentoring at Work: Developmental Relationships in Organizational Life (Scott Foresman, 1985); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Develops future leads across teams; shapes hiring and onboarding.
  — *Why this level:* Extending mentoring's career-development function to produce future leads across multiple teams -- and codifying it into how the org hires and onboards -- is SFIA's higher-responsibility band of defining practice others follow, beyond Kram's single-relationship unit of analysis. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kram, Mentoring at Work: Developmental Relationships in Organizational Life (Scott Foresman, 1985).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Develops senior engineers and leaders; builds culture deliberately.
  — *Why this level:* Deliberately building a mentoring culture -- not just running individual developmental relationships -- is the organization-wide authority SFIA's top responsibility bands describe: setting the standard other leaders' development practice is measured against. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kram, Mentoring at Work: Developmental Relationships in Organizational Life (Scott Foresman, 1985).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Develops the next generation of top talent; legacy outlasts tenure.
  — *Why this level:* A development practice whose output (the talent it produced) persists after the person who built it has left is Dreyfus's master band: the practitioner's judgment becomes the reference point rather than needing the practitioner present, matching SFIA's highest level of setting organizational direction with lasting effect. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

<a id="li-02"></a>
##### LI-02 — Hiring & Staffing

*Type:* Behavioral — Builds the team through hiring and placement.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Participates in interviews; gives clear, evidence-based feedback.
  — *Why this level:* Giving evidence-based interview feedback under someone else's process design is applying a supplied structured-evaluation method rather than designing one -- Schmidt & Hunter's meta-analysis shows structured, evidence-based judgment is what makes interview signal valid at all, and using it under guidance is Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Schmidt & Hunter, The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology, Psychological Bulletin 124(2), 262-274 (1998).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Runs interviews well; calibrates against a consistent bar.
  — *Why this level:* Running interviews independently and calibrating to a consistent bar is exactly the structured-interviewing discipline Google's re:Work guide operationalizes; doing it unsupervised for routine hires is the advanced-beginner band, applying a recognized method without yet designing one. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Google re:Work, Guide: Use Structured Interviewing (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Shapes hiring for a team; designs loops; makes sound staffing calls.
  — *Why this level:* Designing an interview loop -- choosing which structured signals to collect and how to combine them -- rather than following one, is the autonomous, ambiguity-handling competent band; it requires the same validity judgment Schmidt & Hunter's research quantifies, applied to a team's specific hiring problem. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Google re:Work, Guide: Use Structured Interviewing (accessed 2026-07); Schmidt & Hunter, The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology, Psychological Bulletin 124(2), 262-274 (1998).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Drives hiring strategy across teams; builds the interviewing bar.
  — *Why this level:* Building the interviewing bar multiple teams adopt, rather than running one team's loop, is SFIA's higher-responsibility band of defining the approach others follow -- the org-wide analog of re:Work's single-team structured-interviewing guide. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Google re:Work, Guide: Use Structured Interviewing (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the org's talent strategy.
  — *Why this level:* Setting talent strategy for an entire org -- workforce planning, leveling, sourcing priorities -- is SFIA's authority band: anticipating direction and setting standards rather than executing within them. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Shapes company-wide talent philosophy.
  — *Why this level:* A talent philosophy that shapes how an entire company thinks about hiring, outlasting any one leader's tenure, is Dreyfus's master band and SFIA's highest responsibility level -- the practitioner's judgment becomes doctrine rather than decision. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

#### Technical Leadership

<a id="li-03"></a>
##### LI-03 — Technical Influence & Direction

*Type:* Behavioral — Shapes technical direction beyond own work.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Contributes informed opinions in technical discussions.
  — *Why this level:* Contributing informed opinions without yet being the one others defer to is Dreyfus's novice band -- participation under the umbrella of others' technical judgment, not independent influence. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Influences component-level decisions through credibility.
  — *Why this level:* Earning influence over a component through demonstrated competence rather than title is the tech-lead credibility Fournier's Manager's Path identifies as the first rung of technical leadership; doing it for one's own component, independently, is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Fournier, The Manager's Path (O'Reilly, 2017).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Sets technical direction for a domain; others align to their calls.
  — *Why this level:* Being the person a domain's technical calls default to -- Larson's 'Solver'/'Tech Lead' archetype operating with full autonomy over ambiguous problems -- is the competent band: the local go-to, handling hard cases unsupervised. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Larson, Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track (self-published, 2021).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Shapes how multiple teams approach problems; trusted tiebreaker.
  — *Why this level:* Serving as the trusted tiebreaker across multiple teams, shaping shared technical approach rather than one domain's, is Larson's 'Architect' scope crossing team boundaries -- SFIA's higher band of defining direction others adopt rather than following one. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Larson, Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track (self-published, 2021).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Influences org-wide technical strategy.
  — *Why this level:* Influencing technical strategy at the level of an entire org -- the 'Right Hand'/distinguished-engineer altitude Larson describes advising executives -- is SFIA's authority band: anticipating direction and setting standards for a whole organization, not one cross-team problem. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Larson, Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track (self-published, 2021).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Influences company strategic direction through insight.
  — *Why this level:* Technical insight that reshapes company strategy itself, not just its technical execution, is Dreyfus's master band -- judgment operating at the altitude SFIA reserves for its highest responsibility level, where the individual sets direction the whole enterprise follows. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

<a id="li-04"></a>
##### LI-04 — Decision-Making under Uncertainty

*Type:* Behavioral — Makes sound calls with incomplete information.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Makes well-defined decisions; asks good questions when blocked.
  — *Why this level:* Deciding well inside well-defined boundaries and knowing when to ask rather than guess is Dreyfus's novice band exactly as defined: rule-following competence plus the judgment to seek help outside the rules' coverage. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Decides independently within their components; evaluates alternatives honestly.
  — *Why this level:* Independently weighing alternatives for scoped, familiar decisions is the early stage of the recognition-primed judgment Klein documents -- pattern-matching against a smaller base of experience than a domain expert has, which Dreyfus places at advanced-beginner. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Klein, Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions (MIT Press, 1998).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Makes architectural choices for a domain that hold up over months.
  — *Why this level:* Choices that hold up over months under incomplete information are decisions made in Snowden & Boone's 'complicated' or 'complex' Cynefin domains, where good practice replaces best practice; making them autonomously, drawing on the deep experience base Klein's naturalistic decision-making research describes, is the competent band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Klein, Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions (MIT Press, 1998); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review (Nov 2007).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Foresees second-order consequences; sets decision frameworks for teams.
  — *Why this level:* Building the decision frameworks other teams use -- not just making individual good calls -- is the same shift Snowden & Boone describe from applying Cynefin oneself to teaching leaders to diagnose which domain they're in; SFIA's higher band matches this move from decision-maker to framework-definer. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review (Nov 2007).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets decision-making frameworks for the org.
  — *Why this level:* Setting decision frameworks at organizational scale -- choosing which contexts call for best-practice governance versus emergent-practice experimentation, per Snowden & Boone's chaotic/complex distinction -- is SFIA's authority band of org-wide standard-setting. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Snowden & Boone, A Leader's Framework for Decision Making, Harvard Business Review (Nov 2007).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Visionary judgment; sees structural causes others miss.
  — *Why this level:* Seeing structural causes others miss is the master-level intuitive expertise Klein's research identifies as inaccessible to less experienced decision-makers -- pattern recognition so deep it looks like vision, matching Dreyfus's highest band where rules disappear entirely into judgment. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Klein, Sources of Power: How People Make Decisions (MIT Press, 1998).

<a id="li-05"></a>
##### LI-05 — Driving Alignment

*Type:* Behavioral — Gets people moving in the same direction.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Keeps own work aligned with team goals.
  — *Why this level:* Keeping one's own work aligned to goals set by others is Dreyfus's novice band -- compliance with a direction one did not set, not yet the practice of aligning other people. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Aligns direct partners on scoped decisions.
  — *Why this level:* Aligning a small set of direct partners on a scoped decision is Kotter's 'short-term wins' step of change leadership operating at the smallest scale -- doing it independently and routinely is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Drives alignment across a domain; turns disagreement into committed direction.
  — *Why this level:* Turning open disagreement into committed direction across a domain is Kotter's 'guiding coalition' and 'communicate the vision' steps executed autonomously for ambiguous, contested situations -- the competent band's hallmark of handling what routine work doesn't cover. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Aligns multiple teams and leadership behind a direction.
  — *Why this level:* Aligning multiple teams and leadership -- not one domain -- behind a direction is Kotter's full eight-step change model operating at cross-team scale; SFIA's higher responsibility band captures the same shift from domain alignment to defining the approach others adopt. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Creates forums/narratives through which the org aligns.
  — *Why this level:* Building the standing forums and narratives an organization uses to align -- the institutionalization Kotter's final step calls anchoring change in culture -- is SFIA's authority band: setting the mechanism, not just winning one alignment fight. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Aligns the company behind direction; externally persuasive.
  — *Why this level:* Alignment that reaches outside the company -- persuading external stakeholders as well as internal ones -- is Dreyfus's master band operating beyond the organization's boundary, the same externally-referenced altitude SFIA reserves for its top level. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

<a id="li-06"></a>
##### LI-06 — Technical Credibility

*Type:* Behavioral — Retains enough hands-on technical depth to earn engineers' trust, ask the questions that change designs, and judge technical work without doing it.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Follows the team's technical discussions and asks clarifying questions; relies on others to evaluate design quality.
  — *Why this level:* Following discussion and relying on others' design judgment is Dreyfus's novice band precisely: understanding enough to ask questions, not yet enough to be the one whose judgment is trusted. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Understands the systems in scope well enough to review designs, probe trade-offs, and triage incidents — earns technical respect without taking the keyboard.
  — *Why this level:* Reviewing designs and triaging incidents without taking the keyboard is Fournier's description of the tech-lead's shift from doing the work to evaluating others' work -- independent, routine-case competence, which Dreyfus places at advanced-beginner. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Fournier, The Manager's Path (O'Reilly, 2017).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Maintains depth across a complex system's stack and hardest problems; a credible thought-partner to the most senior engineers, pairing them with the context they need.
  — *Why this level:* Being a credible thought-partner to the most senior engineers on the hardest problems in a system is Larson's Staff Engineer 'stay technical' pillar functioning at full autonomy -- the competent band's go-to status for hard, ambiguous cases. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Larson, Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track (self-published, 2021).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Retains broad credibility across a multi-team domain — credible on its hardest cross-cutting technical questions, current enough to ask the question that changes a design.
  — *Why this level:* Credibility that holds across a multi-team domain's hardest cross-cutting questions, current enough to change a design, is Larson's Architect-scope credibility; SFIA's higher band matches the jump from one system's depth to setting technical direction others adopt across teams. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Larson, Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track (self-published, 2021).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sustains the credibility to guide an organization's technology direction; translates architectural risk into business terms without distortion, and senior technologists accept the judgment.
  — *Why this level:* Translating architectural risk into business terms that guide an entire organization's technology direction is Larson's distinguished-engineer altitude advising executives; SFIA's authority band is exactly this: anticipating direction and setting standards at organizational scale. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Larson, Staff Engineer: Leadership Beyond the Management Track (self-published, 2021).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Sustains credibility across an entire technology landscape; their technical judgment is trusted at every altitude because it survives contact with detail.
  — *Why this level:* Judgment trusted at every altitude because it survives contact with detail, across an entire technology landscape, is Dreyfus's master band -- expertise so integrated it needs no external validation -- matching SFIA's highest responsibility level. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

#### Organizational Influence

<a id="li-07"></a>
##### LI-07 — Influence without Authority

*Type:* Behavioral — Wins outcomes across organizational seams with no formal mandate — exchange in others' currencies, coalition-building, and earned credibility.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Builds working relationships with adjacent teams; asks for help through the right people with guidance.
  — *Why this level:* Building relationships and asking for help through the right people, with guidance, is the entry point into Cohen & Bradford's Exchange Model before a person can identify others' currencies unaided -- Dreyfus's novice band, following a supplied approach. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cohen & Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2017).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Wins cooperation from adjacent teams by trading in their currencies — timing help, review effort, shared credit — rather than escalating.
  — *Why this level:* Trading in others' currencies -- timing, review effort, shared credit -- instead of escalating is Cohen & Bradford's Exchange Model applied independently to routine cross-team asks; Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band covers exactly this unaided-but-standard application. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cohen & Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2017).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Secures priority from other teams for an initiative with no borrowed authority; builds the case in the other party's terms and repays visibly.
  — *Why this level:* Building a case in the other party's own terms and repaying visibly is Cialdini's reciprocity and framing principles combined with Cohen & Bradford's currency exchange, applied to a genuinely contested ask -- the competent band's handling of ambiguous, high-stakes influence without any fallback authority. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cohen & Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2017); Cialdini, Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (William Morrow, 1984).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Moves a multi-team domain to a shared position with no mandate — assembles the coalition, converts the best-argued skeptic — and the position holds after they stop pushing.
  — *Why this level:* Assembling a coalition across a multi-team domain and converting the strongest skeptic, so the position holds after the pushing stops, is Cohen & Bradford's currency-exchange model scaled past any single relationship -- SFIA's higher band of shaping outcomes others sustain independently. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Cohen & Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2017).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Shifts organization-level outcomes through people several seams away who advocate the position as their own; lands decisions while holding a minority of the formal power in the room.
  — *Why this level:* Outcomes carried by people several seams away who now argue the position as their own is influence so thoroughly transferred it no longer traces to its source -- SFIA's authority band of org-wide impact achieved without formal power in the room. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Cohen & Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2017).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Shapes industry and market context in the organization's favor — standards bodies, open ecosystems, talent narratives — so external forces push where the organization wants to go.
  — *Why this level:* Shaping standards bodies and market narratives so external forces push in the organization's favor is influence operating beyond the org chart entirely -- Dreyfus's master band and SFIA's highest level both describe judgment whose reach extends past any employer. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

#### Personal Leadership

<a id="li-08"></a>
##### LI-08 — Situational & Adaptive Leadership

*Type:* Behavioral — Reads what the person, team, and moment need and flexes leadership approach — directing, coaching, supporting, delegating — from a grounded, authentic center; distinguishes technical from adaptive challenges.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Recognizes that different people need different support; adjusts approach when prompted by feedback.
  — *Why this level:* Recognizing that people need different support and adjusting only when prompted is the pre-diagnostic stage of Hersey & Blanchard's situational model -- awareness of the four styles without yet reading readiness unaided, which Dreyfus places at the novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Hersey & Blanchard, Management of Organizational Behavior: Utilizing Human Resources (Prentice-Hall, 1969).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Matches direction and support to each person's readiness per task — directing, coaching, supporting, or delegating deliberately — and tells technical problems from adaptive ones.
  — *Why this level:* Deliberately matching directing/coaching/supporting/delegating to a person's readiness per task is Hersey & Blanchard's Situational Leadership model applied independently for routine cases -- Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band, using the named framework as given. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Hersey & Blanchard, Management of Organizational Behavior: Utilizing Human Resources (Prentice-Hall, 1969).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Flexes skillfully across a wide range of people and hard situations without losing a grounded center; refuses to force technical fixes onto adaptive challenges and names the difference.
  — *Why this level:* Naming the difference between technical and adaptive challenges and refusing to force a technical fix onto an adaptive one is Heifetz, Grashow & Linsky's central diagnostic move; doing it skillfully across hard, varied situations without a script is the competent band -- autonomous handling of what no fixed style covers. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Hersey & Blanchard, Management of Organizational Behavior: Utilizing Human Resources (Prentice-Hall, 1969); Heifetz, Grashow & Linsky, The Practice of Adaptive Leadership (Harvard Business Press, 2009).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Coaches other leaders to read what a person, team, or moment needs; adapts across diverse teams while staying recognizably consistent in values.
  — *Why this level:* Coaching other leaders to make Heifetz's technical-versus-adaptive diagnosis themselves, rather than making every call personally, is SFIA's higher band of defining the approach others adopt -- teaching the discipline, not just practicing it. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Heifetz, Grashow & Linsky, The Practice of Adaptive Leadership (Harvard Business Press, 2009).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Develops adaptive leadership as an organizational discipline — leaders diagnose technical-versus-adaptive at scale, and the leadership style changes when the situation does.
  — *Why this level:* Institutionalizing technical-versus-adaptive diagnosis so it happens at organizational scale, not leader-by-leader, is Heifetz's own prescription for organizations facing sustained adaptive work -- SFIA's authority band of setting standards the whole org follows. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Heifetz, Grashow & Linsky, The Practice of Adaptive Leadership (Harvard Business Press, 2009).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Shapes an adaptive, grounded leadership culture across an organization — style stays plastic to conditions while values stay fixed; the approach is emulated beyond the organization.
  — *Why this level:* A leadership culture that stays plastic to conditions while its values stay fixed, and is emulated outside the organization that built it, is Dreyfus's master band operating at SFIA's highest responsibility level -- practice that has become a reference point beyond its origin. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).

<a id="li-09"></a>
##### LI-09 — Self-Awareness & Learning Agility

*Type:* Behavioral — Seeks external feedback on their own behavior, knows their failure patterns, and extracts lessons from first-time situations fast enough to lead credibly in them.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Accepts feedback about their own behavior without defensiveness; acts on it when the change is spelled out.
  — *Why this level:* Accepting feedback without defensiveness and acting on it once spelled out is the receptive precondition Eurich's research identifies before internal self-awareness can develop -- Dreyfus's novice band, following a change others define. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Eurich, What Self-Awareness Really Is (and How to Cultivate It), Harvard Business Review (2018).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Asks for feedback on their own practice and changes visibly in response — "you said X, I changed Y" — keeping a running list of their own failure patterns.
  — *Why this level:* Actively soliciting feedback and visibly changing in response is Eurich's external self-awareness in independent practice; keeping a running list of one's own failure patterns is the growth-mindset habit Dweck documents as distinct from fixed-mindset avoidance of self-scrutiny -- both, done unaided for routine situations, are the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Eurich, What Self-Awareness Really Is (and How to Cultivate It), Harvard Business Review (2018); Dweck, Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (Random House, 2006).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Knows their failure modes under pressure and manages them in the moment; staffs deliberately against known weaknesses and seeks disconfirming input before hard calls.
  — *Why this level:* Managing known failure modes in the moment and seeking disconfirming input before a hard call is the combination of Eurich's internal self-awareness with the self-reflective dimension De Meuse, Dai & Hallenbeck's construct identifies as core to learning agility -- exercised autonomously under real pressure, the competent band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Eurich, What Self-Awareness Really Is (and How to Cultivate It), Harvard Business Review (2018); De Meuse, Dai & Hallenbeck, Learning Agility: A Construct Whose Time Has Come, Consulting Psychology Journal: Practice and Research 62(2), 119-130 (2010).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Runs structured input on themselves — 360s, skip-level themes — and closes the loop publicly on what changed; retools openly for first-time challenges so others copy the learning method.
  — *Why this level:* Running structured self-input mechanisms and retooling openly for first-time challenges so others copy the method is the modeling function De Meuse et al.'s learning-agility research identifies as separating high performers from merely reflective ones -- SFIA's higher band of defining a practice others adopt. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); De Meuse, Dai & Hallenbeck, Learning Agility: A Construct Whose Time Has Come, Consulting Psychology Journal: Practice and Research 62(2), 119-130 (2010).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Compensates deliberately for the seniority feedback vacuum — cultivates truth-tellers, rewards bearers of unwelcome news about themselves, and retires their own outdated playbook when the organization outgrows it.
