  — *Why this level:* Providing decisive counsel on ambiguous, high-stakes business questions autonomously as the trusted go-to advisor is Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band — no case needs a second opinion before the business acts. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines advisory frameworks balancing legal risk and business value that others adopt.
  — *Why this level:* Defining advisory frameworks balancing legal risk and business value that others adopt is SFIA level 5 'Ensure, advise' — authoritative guidance accountable across the business, not one deal. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the model for embedded legal partnering; anticipates business and legal-risk shifts.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the model for embedded legal partnering and anticipating business and legal-risk shifts is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — organization-wide practice design. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines business-partnering best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining business-partnering best practice recognized across the field is the Rule 1.1 commentary's 'lawyer of established competence in the field' ceiling, Dreyfus mastery recognized beyond any one company. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); American Bar Association, Model Rules of Professional Conduct (accessed 2026-07).

### Enterprise Risk, Audit & Governance (RISK)

#### Enterprise Risk Management

<a id="risk-01"></a>
##### RISK-01 — Enterprise risk management

*Type:* Technical — Identify, assess, treat, and monitor risks across the organization within a risk appetite.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Maintains risk registers and gathers risk data under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Maintaining risk registers and gathering data under supervision is COSO ERM's control-activities mechanics performed without ownership of the framework — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Conducts standard risk assessments and updates registers independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Conducting standard risk assessments and updating registers independently with normal review applies COSO ERM's 'Risk Assessment' component to routine risks — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Assesses complex, interconnected enterprise risks and sets local methodology autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Assessing complex, interconnected enterprise risks and setting local methodology autonomously is running ISO 31000's full risk-management process (identification through treatment) unsupervised — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Designs the enterprise risk framework and appetite model others adopt; solves the hardest risk problems.
  — *Why this level:* Designing the enterprise risk framework and appetite model other teams adopt is authoring COSO ERM's 'Strategy and Objective-Setting' and 'Performance' components organization-wide, at SFIA level 5 accountability. *Sources:* COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise risk strategy and appetite at board level; anticipates emerging systemic risks.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise risk strategy and appetite at board level is ISO 31000's Clause 5 mandate that risk management be 'an integral part of governance' set by top management — SFIA level 6 organizational influence. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines; SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines enterprise-risk practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining enterprise-risk practice recognized industry-wide is Dreyfus mastery exercised at the level COSO's own framework authors operate — shaping how the discipline itself is codified. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017).

<a id="risk-02"></a>
##### RISK-02 — Operational & financial risk assessment

*Type:* Technical — Evaluate process, operational, and financial exposures and recommend mitigating controls.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Collects data and completes defined risk-assessment templates under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Collecting data and completing defined risk-assessment templates under supervision is ISO 31000's risk-identification sub-step performed without design authority over the process — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Performs standard operational and financial risk assessments independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Performing standard operational and financial risk assessments independently with normal review applies ISO 31000's risk-analysis and evaluation steps to routine exposures — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Assesses complex, ambiguous operational and financial risks autonomously; the local expert.
  — *Why this level:* Assessing complex, ambiguous operational and financial risks autonomously as the local expert is running ISO 31000's full analysis-to-evaluation cycle on non-routine risk without escalation — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines assessment methodologies and quantification models others adopt; cracks the hardest analyses.
  — *Why this level:* Defining assessment methodologies and quantification models other teams adopt is authoring the risk-criteria and analysis-method choices ISO 31000 Clause 6.4 leaves to the organization, at SFIA level 5 accountability. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines; SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the organization's risk-assessment approach; anticipates emerging operational and financial exposures.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the organization's risk-assessment approach and anticipating emerging exposures ahead of peers is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — policy-level, not assessment-level, work. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines risk-assessment best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining risk-assessment best practice recognized across the field is Dreyfus mastery exercised at the level practitioners who shape ISO working-group guidance operate — beyond applying the standard to authoring how it's applied. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.

<a id="risk-03"></a>
##### RISK-03 — Third-party & vendor risk

*Type:* Technical — Assess and monitor risks introduced by suppliers, partners, and outsourced relationships.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Completes vendor risk questionnaires and tracks assessments under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Completing vendor risk questionnaires and tracking assessments under supervision is planning-stage data collection within the interagency third-party lifecycle, performed without risk-tiering judgment — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); OCC/Federal Reserve/FDIC, Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (2023).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Conducts standard third-party risk assessments and monitoring independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Conducting standard third-party risk assessments and monitoring independently with normal review is executing the interagency guidance's due-diligence and ongoing-monitoring phases for standard-tier vendors — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); OCC/Federal Reserve/FDIC, Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (2023).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Assesses complex, high-criticality vendor and supply-chain risks autonomously through ambiguity.
  — *Why this level:* Assessing complex, high-criticality vendor and supply-chain risks autonomously through ambiguity is applying the interagency guidance's most intensive oversight expectations — reserved for 'critical activities' — without a supervisor setting the tier: Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* OCC/Federal Reserve/FDIC, Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (2023).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Designs the third-party risk framework and tiering model others adopt; resolves the hardest exposures.
  — *Why this level:* Designing the third-party risk framework and tiering model other teams adopt is authoring the risk-based tiering approach the interagency guidance directs organizations to build themselves, at SFIA level 5 accountability across the vendor portfolio. *Sources:* OCC/Federal Reserve/FDIC, Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (2023); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise third-party risk strategy; anticipates emerging supply-chain and concentration risks.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise third-party risk strategy and anticipating emerging supply-chain and concentration risks is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — board-reporting-level policy per the interagency guidance's governance expectations. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines third-party risk practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining third-party risk practice recognized industry-wide is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose approaches inform interagency and regulatory guidance itself operate — shaping the standard rather than implementing it. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); OCC/Federal Reserve/FDIC, Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (2023).

#### Compliance Program Management

<a id="risk-04"></a>
##### RISK-04 — Regulatory compliance program management

*Type:* Technical — Design and operate programs ensuring ongoing adherence to applicable laws and regulations.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Maintains compliance-program records and supports defined controls under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Maintaining compliance-program records and supporting defined controls under supervision is 'paper program' mechanics performed without design ownership — the floor the DOJ's ECCP explicitly distinguishes from an effective program — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Operates standard compliance-program processes and assessments independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Operating standard compliance-program processes and assessments independently with normal review is executing an already-designed program competently — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band, short of the ECCP's 'well-designed' ownership question. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Runs a full compliance program through ambiguity and complex obligations autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Running a full compliance program through ambiguity and complex obligations autonomously is answering the ECCP's core test — is the program 'adequately resourced and empowered to function effectively' — without a supervisor resolving each gap: Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Designs compliance-program architectures and operating models others adopt; resolves the hardest gaps.
  — *Why this level:* Designing compliance-program architectures and operating models other teams adopt is authoring the risk-assessment-driven program design the ECCP evaluates prosecutors against, at SFIA level 5 accountability across the enterprise. *Sources:* U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise compliance-program strategy; anticipates regulatory shifts ahead of enforcement.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise compliance-program strategy and anticipating regulatory shifts ahead of enforcement is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the board- and C-suite-level 'tone at the top' the ECCP asks prosecutors to evaluate. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines compliance-program best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining compliance-program best practice recognized across the field is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose programs become the benchmark cited when guidance like the ECCP itself is revised. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).

<a id="risk-05"></a>
##### RISK-05 — Compliance monitoring & regulatory reporting

*Type:* Technical — Track obligations, test adherence, and prepare required regulatory submissions.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Compiles monitoring data and prepares routine regulatory reports under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Compiling monitoring data and preparing routine regulatory reports under supervision is data-gathering mechanics without ownership of what gets monitored — Dreyfus's novice band, short of the ECCP's expectation that compliance personnel have 'adequate access to data.' *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Executes standard monitoring and reporting cycles independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Executing standard monitoring and reporting cycles independently with normal review is running an already-designed monitoring plan competently — Dreyfus's advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Designs monitoring for complex obligations and resolves ambiguous reporting questions autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Designing monitoring for complex obligations and resolving ambiguous reporting questions autonomously is building the monitoring-and-testing function the ECCP asks whether a program 'is being tested periodically' by — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines monitoring and reporting methodologies others adopt; solves the hardest data and interpretation problems.
  — *Why this level:* Defining monitoring and reporting methodologies other teams adopt, and solving the hardest data problems, is SFIA level 5 accountability for the monitoring architecture across the enterprise, not one reporting cycle. *Sources:* U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise monitoring and reporting strategy; anticipates shifts in regulatory expectations.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise monitoring and reporting strategy and anticipating shifts in regulatory expectations is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — policy ahead of the next examination cycle. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines compliance-monitoring best practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining compliance-monitoring best practice recognized industry-wide is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose methodologies inform how monitoring expectations in guidance like the ECCP evolve. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).

#### Internal Audit & Controls

<a id="risk-06"></a>
##### RISK-06 — Internal audit & controls assurance

*Type:* Technical — Plan and execute independent audits to assess control effectiveness and provide assurance.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Executes defined audit test steps and documents results under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Executing defined audit test steps and documenting results under supervision is first-line-adjacent task execution without the independence the IIA's Three Lines Model reserves for internal audit's third-line role — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); The Institute of Internal Auditors, The IIA's Three Lines Model: An Update of the Three Lines of Defense (2020).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Conducts standard audits and assurance procedures independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Conducting standard audits and assurance procedures independently with normal review is performing the third line's core assurance work on routine engagements — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); The Institute of Internal Auditors, The IIA's Three Lines Model: An Update of the Three Lines of Defense (2020).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Leads complex, high-risk audits and resolves contested findings autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Leading complex, high-risk audits and resolving contested findings autonomously is exercising the organizational independence and objectivity the Three Lines Model requires of internal audit without a supervisor mediating disputed conclusions — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* The Institute of Internal Auditors, The IIA's Three Lines Model: An Update of the Three Lines of Defense (2020).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines audit methodologies and risk-based approaches others adopt; cracks the hardest engagements.
  — *Why this level:* Defining audit methodologies and risk-based approaches other auditors adopt is authoring the audit function's own risk-based methodology, at SFIA level 5 accountability across the audit plan rather than one engagement. *Sources:* The Institute of Internal Auditors, The IIA's Three Lines Model: An Update of the Three Lines of Defense (2020); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise audit strategy and assurance model; anticipates emerging assurance needs.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise audit strategy and assurance model, and anticipating emerging assurance needs, is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the audit-committee-facing strategy work above any single audit. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines internal-audit practice recognized across the profession; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining internal-audit practice recognized across the profession is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners who shape IIA standards and models — like the Three Lines Model's own authors — operate. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); The Institute of Internal Auditors, The IIA's Three Lines Model: An Update of the Three Lines of Defense (2020).

<a id="risk-07"></a>
##### RISK-07 — Internal controls design & testing

*Type:* Technical — Define, document, and test control frameworks that mitigate key business risks.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Documents controls and executes defined test scripts under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Documenting controls and executing defined test scripts under supervision is control-activity mechanics without design ownership — Dreyfus's novice band, short of COSO's expectation that control design itself be evaluated. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); COSO, Internal Control-Integrated Framework (2013).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Designs and tests standard controls independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Designing and testing standard controls independently with normal review applies COSO's Control Activities component to routine processes — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); COSO, Internal Control-Integrated Framework (2013).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Designs controls for complex processes and resolves ambiguous design gaps autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Designing controls for complex processes and resolving ambiguous design gaps autonomously is exercising judgment across COSO's five components (environment, assessment, activities, information, monitoring) without escalation — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* COSO, Internal Control-Integrated Framework (2013).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines control-design frameworks and testing methodologies others adopt; solves the hardest control problems.
  — *Why this level:* Defining control-design frameworks and testing methodologies other teams adopt is authoring the entity-level application of COSO's 17 principles, at SFIA level 5 accountability across the control environment. *Sources:* COSO, Internal Control-Integrated Framework (2013); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise control-environment strategy; anticipates emerging control and automation needs.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise control-environment strategy and anticipating emerging control and automation needs is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the board-reporting-level ownership COSO assigns to senior management. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines controls-design best practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining controls-design best practice recognized industry-wide is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose approaches inform how frameworks like COSO's own Internal Control-Integrated Framework are interpreted and updated. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); COSO, Internal Control-Integrated Framework (2013).

#### Governance, Policy & Ethics

<a id="risk-08"></a>
##### RISK-08 — Policy & standards governance

*Type:* Technical — Develop, approve, and maintain enterprise policies, standards, and their lifecycle.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Drafts routine policy updates from templates and tracks versions under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Drafting routine policy updates from templates and tracking versions under supervision is documentation mechanics without design ownership of the policy framework ISO 31000 asks top management to mandate — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Develops and maintains standard policies and standards independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Developing and maintaining standard policies and standards independently with normal review is applying an already-designed governance framework to routine updates — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Resolves ambiguous, cross-functional policy conflicts and authors complex standards autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Resolving ambiguous, cross-functional policy conflicts and authoring complex standards autonomously is exercising the framework-design judgment ISO 31000 Clause 5 assigns to those integrating risk management into governance — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Designs the policy-governance framework and lifecycle others adopt; resolves the hardest policy tensions.
  — *Why this level:* Designing the policy-governance framework and lifecycle other teams adopt is authoring the mandate-and-commitment structure ISO 31000 requires top management to establish, at SFIA level 5 accountability across the enterprise's policy set. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines; SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise policy-governance strategy; anticipates emerging policy and standards needs.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise policy-governance strategy and anticipating emerging policy needs is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the top-management ownership ISO 31000 places above any single policy. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines policy-governance best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining policy-governance best practice recognized across the field is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose governance models inform how standards like ISO 31000 itself are revised. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management - Guidelines.

<a id="risk-09"></a>
##### RISK-09 — Ethics & conduct program management

*Type:* Behavioral — Foster ethical conduct through codes, training, and a culture of integrity.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Supports ethics-program operations and tracks training and disclosures under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Supporting ethics-program operations and tracking training and disclosures under supervision is administrative mechanics without ownership of the culture-and-tone question the ECCP asks prosecutors to evaluate — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Operates standard ethics and conduct processes independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Operating standard ethics and conduct processes independently with normal review is running an already-designed program's routine cycle — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Handles complex, sensitive conduct matters and ambiguous ethical questions autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Handling complex, sensitive conduct matters and ambiguous ethical questions autonomously is exercising the judgment the ECCP's anti-retaliation and reporting-culture questions assume a program owner exercises — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Designs ethics-program architecture and culture measures others adopt; resolves the hardest dilemmas.
  — *Why this level:* Designing ethics-program architecture and culture measures other teams adopt is authoring the whistleblower-protection and reporting-culture design the 2024 ECCP update specifically evaluates, at SFIA level 5 accountability enterprise-wide. *Sources:* U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise ethics strategy and tone-at-the-top approach; anticipates emerging conduct risks.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise ethics strategy and tone-at-the-top approach, and anticipating emerging conduct risks, is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the C-suite-level ownership the ECCP names directly. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines ethics-program best practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining ethics-program best practice recognized industry-wide is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose program designs inform how guidance like the ECCP itself evolves on conduct and culture. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); U.S. Department of Justice, Criminal Division, Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs (Updated September 2024).

<a id="risk-10"></a>
##### RISK-10 — Fraud prevention & investigations

*Type:* Technical — Detect, investigate, and respond to fraud, misconduct, and integrity violations.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Gathers evidence and documents investigation steps under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Gathering evidence and documenting investigation steps under supervision is fieldwork execution without case-strategy ownership — Dreyfus's novice band, short of the fraud-examiner judgment ACFE's body of knowledge assumes of a lead investigator. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, Report to the Nations: Occupational Fraud (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Conducts standard fraud investigations and control reviews independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Conducting standard fraud investigations and control reviews independently with normal review applies ACFE's standard examination methodology to routine schemes — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, Report to the Nations: Occupational Fraud (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Leads complex, high-stakes investigations and ambiguous fraud schemes autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Leading complex, high-stakes investigations and ambiguous fraud schemes autonomously is exercising the case-strategy judgment ACFE's Report to the Nations attributes to experienced examiners on novel schemes — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, Report to the Nations: Occupational Fraud (accessed 2026-07).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines investigation methodologies and fraud-detection frameworks others adopt; cracks the hardest cases.
  — *Why this level:* Defining investigation methodologies and fraud-detection frameworks other investigators adopt is authoring the organization's detection methodology against the scheme patterns ACFE's Report to the Nations tracks, at SFIA level 5 accountability. *Sources:* Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, Report to the Nations: Occupational Fraud (accessed 2026-07); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise fraud-risk strategy; anticipates emerging fraud schemes and exposures.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise fraud-risk strategy and anticipating emerging fraud schemes and exposures is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — proactive policy, not case investigation. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines fraud-investigation best practice recognized across the profession; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining fraud-investigation best practice recognized across the profession is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose casework and methodology inform ACFE's own published benchmarks operate. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Association of Certified Fraud Examiners, Report to the Nations: Occupational Fraud (accessed 2026-07).

#### Resilience & Continuity

<a id="risk-11"></a>
##### RISK-11 — Business continuity & resilience

*Type:* Technical — Plan and maintain capabilities to sustain and recover critical operations during disruption.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Maintains continuity documentation and supports defined exercises under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Maintaining continuity documentation and supporting defined exercises under supervision is documentation mechanics without ownership of the business-impact-analysis judgment ISO 22301 requires — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 22301:2019 Security and Resilience - Business Continuity Management Systems - Requirements (2019).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Develops standard continuity plans and runs routine exercises independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Developing standard continuity plans and running routine exercises independently with normal review applies ISO 22301's plan-and-exercise cycle to known-pattern operations — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 22301:2019 Security and Resilience - Business Continuity Management Systems - Requirements (2019).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Designs resilience for complex, interdependent operations and resolves ambiguous gaps autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Designing resilience for complex, interdependent operations and resolving ambiguous gaps autonomously is running ISO 22301's full business-impact-analysis-to-exercising cycle for non-routine dependencies without escalation — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 22301:2019 Security and Resilience - Business Continuity Management Systems - Requirements (2019).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines the resilience framework and impact-analysis methodology others adopt; solves the hardest scenarios.
  — *Why this level:* Defining the resilience framework and impact-analysis methodology other teams adopt is authoring the business continuity management system ISO 22301 requires top management to establish, at SFIA level 5 accountability across the enterprise's operations. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 22301:2019 Security and Resilience - Business Continuity Management Systems - Requirements (2019); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise resilience strategy; anticipates emerging disruption and concentration risks.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise resilience strategy and anticipating emerging disruption and concentration risks is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the top-management ownership ISO 22301 assigns above any single plan. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines resilience best practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining resilience best practice recognized industry-wide is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose management-system designs inform how standards like ISO 22301 itself are revised. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 22301:2019 Security and Resilience - Business Continuity Management Systems - Requirements (2019).

<a id="risk-12"></a>
##### RISK-12 — Crisis management & response coordination

*Type:* Behavioral — Coordinate organizational response, decision-making, and communication during crisis events.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Supports crisis logistics and documentation under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Supporting crisis logistics and documentation under supervision is task execution without the decision-making role ISO 22361 reserves for the crisis team — Dreyfus's novice band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 22361:2022 Security and Resilience - Crisis Management - Guidelines (2022).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Coordinates defined crisis-response tasks and communications independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Coordinating defined crisis-response tasks and communications independently with normal review is executing an already-designed response plan competently — the Dreyfus advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 22361:2022 Security and Resilience - Crisis Management - Guidelines (2022).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Leads response for complex, fast-moving crises and ambiguous decisions autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Leading response for complex, fast-moving crises and ambiguous decisions autonomously is exercising the decision-making-under-uncertainty judgment ISO 22361 assigns to crisis leadership without a supervisor resolving each call — Dreyfus's competent-to-proficient band. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 22361:2022 Security and Resilience - Crisis Management - Guidelines (2022).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines crisis-response frameworks and command structures others adopt; steers the hardest crises.
  — *Why this level:* Defining crisis-response frameworks and command structures other teams adopt is authoring the governance-and-leadership structure ISO 22361 requires organizations to design themselves, at SFIA level 5 accountability enterprise-wide. *Sources:* ISO, ISO 22361:2022 Security and Resilience - Crisis Management - Guidelines (2022); SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise crisis-management strategy; anticipates emerging crisis scenarios and readiness gaps.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise crisis-management strategy and anticipating emerging crisis scenarios and readiness gaps is SFIA level 6 'Initiate, influence' — the top-management strategic responsibility ISO 22361 names directly. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines crisis-management best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Defining crisis-management best practice recognized across the field is Dreyfus mastery at the level practitioners whose frameworks inform how standards like ISO 22361 itself are written and revised. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); ISO, ISO 22361:2022 Security and Resilience - Crisis Management - Guidelines (2022).

### Corporate Strategy & Executive Leadership (STRAT)

#### Strategy Formulation

<a id="strat-01"></a>
##### STRAT-01 — Corporate strategy formulation

*Type:* Behavioral — Define enterprise direction, scope, and competitive positioning to create durable advantage.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Gathers inputs and assembles analysis for strategy work under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Assembling competitive-analysis inputs and running assigned frameworks under a senior strategist's supervision is Dreyfus's novice band: the analyst follows given rules without discretion over which framework fits the situation. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Develops components of strategy and standard analyses independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Independently applying a structural framework like Porter's Five Forces to a defined market and producing a standard competitive analysis is the advanced-beginner band -- situational pattern-matching within a known method, still normally reviewed. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Porter, Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (Free Press, 1980).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Frames ambiguous strategic problems and shapes coherent strategy autonomously; the go-to strategist.
  — *Why this level:* Framing an ambiguous strategic problem into Rumelt's 'kernel' -- diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action -- without a template to follow is the competent/proficient band: judgment under genuine uncertainty replaces correct execution of known steps. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Rumelt, Good Strategy Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters (Crown Business, 2011).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines strategy-formulation approaches others adopt; resolves the hardest strategic trade-offs.
  — *Why this level:* Turning a personal method for structural industry analysis into a formulation approach other strategists in the org adopt is SFIA's ensure/advise responsibility level -- codifying and teaching a method, not just applying it well. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Porter, Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (Free Press, 1980).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise strategic direction; anticipates major shifts reshaping the competitive landscape.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's strategic direction and anticipating shifts in the competitive landscape ahead of the business is SFIA's initiate/influence level: authority spans the whole organization, not one engagement. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines corporate-strategy practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited thought leader.
  — *Why this level:* Corporate-strategy practice recognized and cited industry-wide -- the position Porter's and Rumelt's own frameworks occupy in the field -- is SFIA's top set-strategy/mobilize level: shaping the discipline beyond any one employer. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Porter, Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (Free Press, 1980); Rumelt, Good Strategy Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters (Crown Business, 2011).

<a id="strat-02"></a>
##### STRAT-02 — Strategic planning & OKR cascading

*Type:* Behavioral — Translate strategy into multi-horizon plans and cascading objectives across the enterprise.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Maintains planning artifacts and tracks objectives under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Maintaining planning artifacts and tracking objectives under supervision is the novice band: executing a defined tracking process without authority to adjust the cascade. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Runs standard planning cycles and cascades objectives independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Running a standard OKR cycle independently -- setting and cascading objectives per Doerr's committed/aspirational OKR mechanics -- with normal review is the advanced-beginner band: correct use of a known method, not designing it. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Doerr, Measure What Matters: How Google, Bono, and the Gates Foundation Rock the World with OKRs (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Designs planning for complex, interdependent units and resolves misalignment autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Designing planning for complex, interdependent units and resolving cross-unit misalignment autonomously -- building a strategy map that links objectives across functions per Kaplan & Norton -- is the competent band: no playbook, judgment under ambiguity. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kaplan & Norton, The Balanced Scorecard: Translating Strategy into Action (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines the planning and goal-cascade methodology others adopt; fixes the hardest alignment failures.
  — *Why this level:* Defining the planning/OKR-cascade methodology that other teams in the org adopt, and fixing the hardest alignment failures, is SFIA's ensure/advise level: the practitioner becomes the method's author, not just its user. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Doerr, Measure What Matters: How Google, Bono, and the Gates Foundation Rock the World with OKRs (Portfolio/Penguin, 2018).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise planning operating model; anticipates shifts in how strategy translates to execution.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's planning operating model and anticipating how strategy-to-execution translation must evolve is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- organization-wide ownership of the planning system itself. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines strategic-planning best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Strategic-planning practice recognized externally as authoritative -- the standing Kaplan & Norton's Balanced Scorecard achieved industry-wide -- is SFIA's top responsibility level: the practitioner's method becomes the field's reference. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kaplan & Norton, The Balanced Scorecard: Translating Strategy into Action (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).

<a id="strat-03"></a>
##### STRAT-03 — Business model & innovation strategy

*Type:* Behavioral — Design and evolve how the organization creates, delivers, and captures value over time.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Researches business models and supports innovation analysis under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Researching business models and supporting innovation analysis under supervision is the novice band: gathering inputs against a given template, not yet forming independent judgment about the model. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Develops standard business-model analyses and innovation cases independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Independently completing a standard Business Model Canvas analysis or innovation case with normal review is the advanced-beginner band -- competent use of Osterwalder & Pigneur's nine building blocks, not inventing new ones. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Osterwalder & Pigneur, Business Model Generation: A Handbook for Visionaries, Game Changers, and Challengers (Wiley, 2010).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Designs novel business models and resolves ambiguous innovation bets autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Designing a novel business model or resolving an ambiguous innovation bet autonomously -- recognizing a disruptive-innovation pattern per Christensen without a precedent to copy -- is the competent/proficient band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Christensen, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail (Harvard Business School Press, 1997).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines business-model and innovation frameworks others adopt; cracks the hardest model problems.
  — *Why this level:* Defining business-model and innovation frameworks that other teams adopt, and cracking the model problems others can't, is SFIA's ensure/advise level: the practitioner's canvas or method becomes the org's standard tool. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Osterwalder & Pigneur, Business Model Generation: A Handbook for Visionaries, Game Changers, and Challengers (Wiley, 2010).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets enterprise business-model and innovation strategy; anticipates disruptive shifts.
  — *Why this level:* Setting enterprise business-model and innovation strategy and anticipating disruptive shifts -- the anticipatory judgment Christensen shows incumbents systematically lack -- is SFIA's initiate/influence level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Christensen, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail (Harvard Business School Press, 1997).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines business-model innovation practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited thought leader.
  — *Why this level:* Business-model-innovation practice recognized industry-wide, in the way the Business Model Canvas became a global standard vocabulary, is SFIA's top set-strategy level: the practitioner's framework outlives any one company. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Osterwalder & Pigneur, Business Model Generation: A Handbook for Visionaries, Game Changers, and Challengers (Wiley, 2010).

<a id="strat-04"></a>
##### STRAT-04 — Scenario planning & strategic foresight

*Type:* Technical — Anticipate future conditions through scenarios and signals to stress-test strategic choices.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Gathers signals and supports scenario documentation under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Gathering signals and supporting scenario documentation under supervision is the novice band: collecting inputs to someone else's scenario framework without discretion over which signals matter. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Builds standard scenarios and trend analyses independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Independently building standard scenarios and trend analyses with normal review is the advanced-beginner band -- competently running Schwartz's eight-step scenario process on a defined question, not yet handling genuinely ambiguous futures. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Schwartz, The Art of the Long View: Planning for the Future in an Uncertain World (Doubleday, 1991).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Constructs complex, ambiguous scenarios and derives strategic implications autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Constructing complex, ambiguous scenarios and deriving strategic implications autonomously is the competent band -- Wack's own distinction between mechanically generating scenarios and using them to change managers' view of reality is exactly the P2-to-P3 jump. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Wack, Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead, Harvard Business Review (September-October 1985).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines foresight methodologies others adopt; surfaces the non-obvious futures others miss.
  — *Why this level:* Defining the foresight methodology other planners adopt and surfacing the non-obvious futures others miss is SFIA's ensure/advise level: authoring the scenario method, not just executing Schwartz's steps well. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Schwartz, The Art of the Long View: Planning for the Future in an Uncertain World (Doubleday, 1991).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise foresight approach; anticipates structural shifts ahead of the market.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's foresight approach and anticipating structural shifts ahead of the market is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- the scope moves from one scenario set to the org's whole future-sensing capability. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines strategic-foresight best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Strategic-foresight practice recognized industry-wide -- the standing Wack's Shell scenario method achieved as the field's founding case study -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Wack, Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead, Harvard Business Review (September-October 1985).

#### Market & Competitive Insight

<a id="strat-05"></a>
##### STRAT-05 — Market & competitive intelligence

*Type:* Technical — Analyze markets, customers, and rivals to inform positioning and strategic moves.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Collects market and competitor data and compiles routine briefs under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Collecting market and competitor data and compiling routine briefs under supervision is the novice band: executing a defined collection task without judgment on what the data implies. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Produces standard competitive analyses and market assessments independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Producing a standard competitive analysis independently with normal review -- correctly applying Five Forces or comparable structural analysis to a known industry -- is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Porter, Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (Free Press, 1980).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Synthesizes ambiguous signals into decisive competitive insight autonomously; the go-to analyst.
  — *Why this level:* Synthesizing ambiguous signals into decisive competitive insight autonomously -- selecting the right analytic technique per Fleisher & Bensoussan's FAROUT method rather than applying one by rote -- is the competent/proficient band; go-to-analyst status follows from that judgment. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Fleisher & Bensoussan, Business and Competitive Analysis: Effective Application of New and Classic Methods, 2nd Edition (FT Press, 2015).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines intelligence methodologies and frameworks others adopt; cracks the hardest market questions.
  — *Why this level:* Defining intelligence methodologies and frameworks other analysts adopt, and cracking the hardest market questions, is SFIA's ensure/advise level: the practitioner's method selection becomes the team's doctrine. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Fleisher & Bensoussan, Business and Competitive Analysis: Effective Application of New and Classic Methods, 2nd Edition (FT Press, 2015).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise intelligence agenda; anticipates competitive and market shifts ahead of rivals.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise intelligence agenda and anticipating competitive shifts ahead of rivals is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- organization-wide anticipatory scope, not one analysis. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines competitive-intelligence best practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Competitive-intelligence best practice recognized industry-wide -- the standing Porter's structural-analysis vocabulary achieved as the field's shared language -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Porter, Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (Free Press, 1980).

#### Corporate Development

<a id="strat-06"></a>
##### STRAT-06 — Mergers, acquisitions & corporate development

*Type:* Technical — Source, evaluate, and integrate inorganic growth opportunities including deals and partnerships.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Compiles target data and supports deal models under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Compiling target data and supporting deal models under supervision is the novice band: executing defined data-gathering tasks with no discretion over deal judgment. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Runs standard screening, modeling, and diligence workstreams independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Running standard screening, modeling, and diligence workstreams independently with normal review -- applying Bruner's established valuation and diligence toolkit to a routine deal -- is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Bruner, Applied Mergers and Acquisitions (Wiley Finance, 2004).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Drives complex deal evaluation, structuring, and negotiation autonomously through ambiguity.
  — *Why this level:* Driving complex deal evaluation, structuring, and negotiation autonomously through ambiguity is the competent band -- Haspeslagh & Jemison's integration-design judgment for step-change acquisitions has no fixed playbook, unlike routine diligence. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Haspeslagh & Jemison, Managing Acquisitions: Creating Value Through Corporate Renewal (Free Press, 1991).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines deal-evaluation and integration frameworks others adopt; resolves the hardest deal problems.
  — *Why this level:* Defining deal-evaluation and integration frameworks other dealmakers adopt, resolving the hardest deal problems, is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's integration-design approach becomes the org's method, per Haspeslagh & Jemison's own prescriptive frame. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Haspeslagh & Jemison, Managing Acquisitions: Creating Value Through Corporate Renewal (Free Press, 1991).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise corporate-development strategy and portfolio direction; anticipates consolidation shifts.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's corporate-development strategy and portfolio direction, anticipating consolidation shifts, is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- scope moves from individual deals to the whole inorganic-growth portfolio. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines corporate-development practice recognized industry-wide; externally credible authority on deals.
  — *Why this level:* Corporate-development practice recognized industry-wide and externally credible on deals -- the standing Bruner's own M&A scholarship achieved as a field reference -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Bruner, Applied Mergers and Acquisitions (Wiley Finance, 2004).

<a id="strat-07"></a>
##### STRAT-07 — Capital allocation & investment prioritization

*Type:* Technical — Allocate scarce capital across initiatives to maximize risk-adjusted enterprise returns.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Compiles investment data and supports prioritization analyses under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Compiling investment data and supporting prioritization analyses under supervision is the novice band: gathering inputs to a given allocation model without discretion over criteria. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Evaluates standard investments and applies allocation criteria independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Evaluating standard investments and applying allocation criteria independently with normal review -- correctly running Koller, Goedhart & Wessels's DCF/ROIC-based evaluation on a routine case -- is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Koller, Goedhart & Wessels, Valuation: Measuring and Managing the Value of Companies, 7th Edition (McKinsey & Company/Wiley, 2020).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Prioritizes complex, competing investments under ambiguity and constraint autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Prioritizing complex, competing investments under ambiguity and constraint autonomously is the competent band: Graham & Harvey's survey shows even experienced CFOs vary in which criteria they weight under real constraints -- resolving that judgment call independently is the P2-to-P3 boundary. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Graham & Harvey, The Theory and Practice of Corporate Finance: Evidence from the Field, Journal of Financial Economics 60(2-3), 187-243 (2001).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines capital-allocation frameworks and hurdle models others adopt; resolves the hardest trade-offs.
  — *Why this level:* Defining capital-allocation frameworks and hurdle models other teams adopt, resolving the hardest trade-offs, is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's allocation method becomes the org's standard, beyond applying Koller et al.'s framework well. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Koller, Goedhart & Wessels, Valuation: Measuring and Managing the Value of Companies, 7th Edition (McKinsey & Company/Wiley, 2020).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise capital-allocation strategy; anticipates shifts in where value is created.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's capital-allocation strategy and anticipating shifts in where value is created is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- portfolio-wide authority, not one investment case. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines capital-allocation best practice recognized across the field; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Capital-allocation best practice recognized across the field -- the standing Graham & Harvey's empirical survey achieved as the reference study of how capital budgeting is actually practiced -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Graham & Harvey, The Theory and Practice of Corporate Finance: Evidence from the Field, Journal of Financial Economics 60(2-3), 187-243 (2001).

<a id="strat-08"></a>
##### STRAT-08 — Business case & financial analysis

*Type:* Technical — Build rigorous financial cases and valuations to justify and compare major investments.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Builds routine financial models and gathers assumptions under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Building routine financial models and gathering assumptions under supervision is the novice band: populating a given model template without discretion over methodology. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Develops standard business cases and analyses independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Developing standard business cases and analyses independently with normal review -- correctly applying Brealey, Myers & Allen's NPV/valuation mechanics to a routine case -- is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance, 13th Edition (McGraw-Hill, 2019).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Constructs rigorous cases for complex, ambiguous decisions autonomously; the go-to analyst.
  — *Why this level:* Constructing rigorous cases for complex, ambiguous decisions autonomously -- choosing among Damodaran's competing valuation models for an asset with no obvious comparable -- is the competent/proficient band; go-to-analyst status follows from that model-selection judgment. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Damodaran, Investment Valuation: Tools and Techniques for Determining the Value of Any Asset, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2012).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines business-case and modeling standards others adopt; cracks the hardest valuation problems.
  — *Why this level:* Defining business-case and modeling standards other analysts adopt, cracking the hardest valuation problems, is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's modeling approach becomes the org's standard rather than a personal skill. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Damodaran, Investment Valuation: Tools and Techniques for Determining the Value of Any Asset, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2012).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise investment-analysis approach; anticipates shifts in value drivers and risk.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's investment-analysis approach and anticipating shifts in value drivers and risk is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- scope spans the whole investment-analysis function. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines business-case and financial-analysis best practice recognized industry-wide; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Business-case and financial-analysis best practice recognized industry-wide -- the standing Brealey, Myers & Allen's text achieved as the field's teaching reference across decades of editions -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance, 13th Edition (McGraw-Hill, 2019).

#### Governance & Enterprise Leadership

<a id="strat-09"></a>
##### STRAT-09 — Board & governance leadership

*Type:* Behavioral — Engage boards and govern the enterprise with accountability, ethics, and fiduciary discipline.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Prepares board materials and tracks governance actions under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Preparing board materials and tracking governance actions under supervision is the novice band: executing defined administrative tasks with no discretion over governance judgment. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Manages standard board processes and reporting independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Managing standard board processes and reporting independently with normal review -- correctly running the disclosure and non-executive-director practices the Cadbury Report codified -- is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Cadbury, Report of the Committee on the Financial Aspects of Corporate Governance (Gee and Co., 1992).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Steers complex board dynamics and ambiguous governance questions autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Steering complex board dynamics and ambiguous governance questions autonomously -- applying the OECD Principles' stakeholder and disclosure guidance to a situation the code doesn't spell out -- is the competent band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); OECD, G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (OECD Publishing, 2015).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines board operating models and governance practices others adopt; resolves the hardest tensions.
  — *Why this level:* Defining board operating models and governance practices other leaders adopt, resolving the hardest tensions, is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- codifying governance practice beyond applying the OECD Principles well. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); OECD, G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (OECD Publishing, 2015).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise governance and board-effectiveness strategy; anticipates governance shifts.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise's governance and board-effectiveness strategy and anticipating governance shifts is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- authority over the whole governance system, not one board cycle. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines board-governance best practice recognized across the field; externally credible authority.
  — *Why this level:* Board-governance best practice recognized across the field and externally credible -- the standing the Cadbury Code achieved as the template later codes worldwide were built from -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Cadbury, Report of the Committee on the Financial Aspects of Corporate Governance (Gee and Co., 1992).

<a id="strat-10"></a>
##### STRAT-10 — Enterprise transformation leadership

*Type:* Behavioral — Lead large-scale, cross-enterprise change to reshape the organization's operating model.

- **[P1 — Assisted](proficiency_scale.md#p1):** Supports transformation tracking and documentation under supervision.
  — *Why this level:* Supporting transformation tracking and documentation under supervision is the novice band: executing defined tracking tasks with no discretion over the change approach. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980).
- **[P2 — Independent](proficiency_scale.md#p2):** Leads defined transformation workstreams independently with normal review.
  — *Why this level:* Leading a defined transformation workstream independently with normal review -- running steps of Kotter's eight-stage change process on a bounded scope -- is the advanced-beginner band. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P3 — Proficient](proficiency_scale.md#p3):** Drives complex, cross-functional transformation through ambiguity and resistance autonomously.
  — *Why this level:* Driving complex, cross-functional transformation through ambiguity and resistance autonomously is the competent band: Kotter's own finding is that most efforts fail precisely where there's no fixed playbook for overcoming entrenched resistance -- succeeding there without one is the P2-to-P3 boundary. *Sources:* Dreyfus & Dreyfus, A Five-Stage Model of the Mental Activities Involved in Directed Skill Acquisition (1980); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P4 — Expert](proficiency_scale.md#p4):** Defines transformation approaches and operating models others adopt; rescues the hardest programs.
  — *Why this level:* Defining transformation approaches and operating models other leaders adopt, rescuing the hardest programs, is SFIA's ensure/advise level -- the practitioner's adaptation of Kotter's model becomes the org's own transformation method. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).
- **[P5 — Authority](proficiency_scale.md#p5):** Sets the enterprise transformation strategy; anticipates the shifts that make transformation necessary.
  — *Why this level:* Setting the enterprise transformation strategy and anticipating the shifts that make transformation necessary is SFIA's initiate/influence level -- scope spans the whole enterprise's change agenda, not one program. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024).
- **[P6 — Pioneer](proficiency_scale.md#p6):** Defines transformation-leadership best practice recognized industry-wide; externally cited authority.
  — *Why this level:* Transformation-leadership practice recognized industry-wide -- the standing Kotter's eight-stage model achieved as the field's default change-management vocabulary -- is SFIA's top set-strategy level. *Sources:* SFIA Foundation, Skills Framework for the Information Age, version 9 (2024); Kotter, Leading Change (Harvard Business School Press, 1996).

### Business & Revenue Operations (BIZ)

#### Operational Excellence

<a id="biz-01"></a>
##### BIZ-01 — Business operations & process improvement
